steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Cloud computing is transforming a large part of the IT industry, since it makes software as a service more attractive and changes how hardware is designed and purchased. It offers unlimited storage and processing power, and unlimited access to resources. Virtualization is a crucial technology that allows hardware resources to be shared efficiently, and it has two main types: virtual machines (VMs), which emulate complete computer systems, and containers, which are lightweight units that share the host operation system kernel so deployment and scalability are more streamlined.

CloudLab is a cloud computing testbed for research and education, and it provides infrastructure to run other platforms, including clusters of virtual machines and containers. The default virtualization mode of Xen is hardware virtual machine (HVM), and CloudLab supports it too. With HVM virtualization, virtual machines operate as virtual hardware devices, so a wide range of operating systems can run at the same time as guest operating systems. To run paravirtualization (PV) mode on CloudLab, you need to provide a script that defines a new profile. In PV, the guest operating system is modified so it is aware of its virtualized environment. This mode often gives better performance since it reduces the virtualization overhead. With these two approaches users can tailor the benefits to their specific requirements.

Container orchestration can be done by Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, or Apache Mesos. Kubernetes is widely known as a clustering platform for running and managing containerized services such as OpenFaaS. Figure 1 shows the Kubernetes architecture. There are several Kubernetes distributions, including Kubeadm, Kubespray, K3s, Rancher, MicroK8s, and K0s. Kubernetes includes a container runtime that manages the life cycle of containers, which means launching, stopping, and monitoring them. When container runtimes use user-space kernels to enforce isolation, the operation of containers can be affected. So container runtime performance is important, because it makes sure containers run properly and efficiently, guarantees system performance, and allows a balanced allocation of computing, storage, and network resources. Figure 2 shows the architectures of Docker and Containerd, which are the two most popular container runtimes.

- FaaS
  - serverless; abstracts infrastructure management; developers focus on code (cite)
  - integrated with containerization; dependencies in containers
  - platform handles provisioning and execution from function code (cite)
  - Knative (cite), Apache OpenWhisk (cite), Fission (cite), Nuclio (cite); OpenFaaS (cite) popular: github stars 24.3k (cite), used by researchers (cite)
  - Figure 3: OpenFaaS architecture
- This study
  - four distributions: Kubeadm, K3s, MicroK8s, K0s
  - Xen efficient hypervisor per related work (cite) -> platform for Kubernetes
  - first HVM vs PV; new CloudLab profile for Xen-PV
  - then Docker vs Containerd; Kubernetes modified to use Docker as alternative; disk and CPU

  - then distributions compared with various metrics
- Organization

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Cloud computing is transforming a large part of the IT industry, since it makes software as a service more attractive and changes how hardware is designed and purchased. It offers unlimited storage and processing power, and unlimited access to resources. Virtualization is a crucial technology that allows hardware resources to be shared efficiently, and it has two main types: virtual machines (VMs), which emulate complete computer systems, and containers, which are lightweight units that share the host operation system kernel so deployment and scalability are more streamlined.

CloudLab is a cloud computing testbed for research and education, and it provides infrastructure to run other platforms, including clusters of virtual machines and containers. The default virtualization mode of Xen is hardware virtual machine (HVM), and CloudLab supports it too. With HVM virtualization, virtual machines operate as virtual hardware devices, so a wide range of operating systems can run at the same time as guest operating systems. To run paravirtualization (PV) mode on CloudLab, you need to provide a script that defines a new profile. In PV, the guest operating system is modified so it is aware of its virtualized environment. This mode often gives better performance since it reduces the virtualization overhead. With these two approaches users can tailor the benefits to their specific requirements.

Container orchestration can be done by Kubernetes, Docker Swarm, or Apache Mesos. Kubernetes is widely known as a clustering platform for running and managing containerized services such as OpenFaaS. Figure 1 shows the Kubernetes architecture. There are several Kubernetes distributions, including Kubeadm, Kubespray, K3s, Rancher, MicroK8s, and K0s. Kubernetes includes a container runtime that manages the life cycle of containers, which means launching, stopping, and monitoring them. When container runtimes use user-space kernels to enforce isolation, the operation of containers can be affected. So container runtime performance is important, because it makes sure containers run properly and efficiently, guarantees system performance, and allows a balanced allocation of computing, storage, and network resources. Figure 2 shows the architectures of Docker and Containerd, which are the two most popular container runtimes.

Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) is a kind of serverless computing that abstracts away the management of the underlying infrastructure, so developers can focus on writing and deploying code. These platforms are usually integrated with containerization technologies, so developers can put their dependencies in containers. A FaaS platform automatically manages resource provisioning and function execution based on the developer's function code. There are many popular FaaS platforms, like Knative, Apache OpenWhisk, Fission, and Nuclio, but OpenFaaS is one of the most popular because of its github stars (24.3k) and because researchers use it a lot. Figure 3 shows the architecture of OpenFaaS.

In this study we evaluate the performance of four Kubernetes distributions, Kubeadm, K3s, MicroK8s, and K0s, from various aspects. Related works have shown that Xen is an efficient hypervisor for virtualization, so we use this hypervisor as the platform for running Kubernetes. First we evaluate the performance of both HVM and PV modes to see which mode performs better. For this, we add a new profile to CloudLab that provides Xen-PV mode on this testbed. After choosing the mode, we investigate Docker and Containerd, two well-known container runtimes that can be integrated with Kubernetes. To do this, we modified Kubernetes so it can also use Docker as an alternative to Containerd, and so we can evaluate both runtimes based on disk and CPU performance. We run Sysbench to compare the runtimes on disk performance when MySQL, which is a disk-intensive application, is deployed on Kubernetes. Then we run OpenFaaS as a compute-intensive application to compare the runtime environments on CPU performance. Once the underlying Xen mode and the container runtime of Kubernetes are chosen, we investigate the performance of the Kubernetes distributions with various metrics.

The rest of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 gives an overview of the research done in this area. Section 3 gives the research methodology and the steps of the experiments. Section 4 describes the experimental setup, including the hardware and software configurations and the benchmarks. Section 5 summarizes the experimental results, including comparisons between the Xen virtualization modes, the container runtimes, and how the Kubernetes distributions perform. Finally, Section 6 gives the final remarks and some future research directions.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Cloud computing is transforming a large part of the IT industry by improving the attractiveness of software as a service, as well as changing how hardware is designed and purchased [1]. It offers unlimited storage and processing power, and unlimited access to resources [2]. Virtualization is a crucial technology allowing for efficient hardware resource sharing, encompassing two main types: virtual machines (VMs), which emulate complete computer systems [3], and containers, lightweight units that share the host operation system kernel for more streamlined deployment and scalability [4,5].

CloudLab [6] is a cloud computing testbed for research and education and provides an infrastructure for running other platforms, including clusters of virtual machines and containers. Xen’s default virtualization mode is hardware virtual machine (HVM), which is also supported by CloudLab. HVM virtualization allows virtual machines to operate as virtual hardware devices, allowing a wide range of operating systems to be executed concurrently as guest operating systems. To run paravirtualization (PV) mode on CloudLab, you need to provide a script to define a new profile. With PV, the guest operating system is modified to be aware of its virtualized environment. This mode often results in better performance as it reduces the overhead of virtualization. With these two approaches, users can tailor the benefits to meet their specific requirements.

Container orchestration can be done by Kubernetes [7], Docker Swarm [8], or Apache Mesos [9,10]. Kubernetes is widely recognized as a clustering platform to run and manage containerized services such as OpenFaaS. Figure 1 shows the Kubernetes architecture. Kubernetes comes in several distributions, including Kubeadm [7], Kubespray [11], K3s [12], Rancher [13], MicroK8s [14], and K0s [15]. It includes a container runtime that manages containers’ life cycles, including launching, stopping, and monitoring them. The operation of containers can be affected when container runtime use user-space kernels to enforce isolation [16]. Therefore, container runtime performance is important as it ensures the proper and efficient execution of containers, guarantees system performance, and enables a balanced allocation of computing, storage, and network resources. Figure 2 shows the architectures of Docker and Containerd [17], the two most popular container runtimes.

Function-as-a-Service (FaaS) is a form of serverless computing that abstracts away the underlying infrastructure management, enabling developers to focus on writing and deploying code [18]. These platforms are usually integrated with containerization technologies, so developers can encapsulate their dependencies in containers. A FaaS platform manages resource provisioning and function execution automatically based on a developer’s function code [19]. There are many popular FaaS platforms, such as Knative [20], Apache OpenWhisk [21], Fission [22], Nuclio [23], but OpenFaaS [24] is one of the most popular due to its github stars (24.3k) [25] and its popularity among researchers [26,27,28,29,30,31,32]. The architecture of OpenFaaS is shown in Figure 3.

This study evaluates the performance of four Kubernetes distributions, namely Kubeadm, K3s, MicroK8s, and K0s, from various aspects. Since related works have shown that Xen is an efficient hypervisor for virtualization [33,34,35,36], this hypervisor is adopted to provide the platform for running Kubernetes. First, we evaluate the performance of both HVM and PV modes to check which mode provides better performance. For this purpose, a new profile is added to CloudLab to provide Xen-PV mode on this testbed. After specifying the appropriate mode, Docker and Containerd, two well-known container runtimes that can be integrated with Kubernetes, are investigated. To this end, Kubernetes has been modified to also use Docker as an alternative to Containerd, so that we can evaluate both runtimes based on disk and CPU performance. We run Sysbench to compare the runtimes in terms of disk performance when MySQL, as a disk-intensive application, is deployed on Kubernetes. Then, OpenFaaS is run as a compute-intensive application to compare runtime environments in terms of CPU performance. Once the underlying Xen mode and the container runtime of Kubernetes are chosen, we investigate the performance of the Kubernetes distributions using various metrics.

The remainder of this article is organized as follows: Section 2 provides an overview of the research conducted in this area. Section 3 provides the research methodology and the steps of the experiments. Section 4 outlines the experimental setup, including hardware and software configurations and the benchmarks. Section 5 summarizes the experimental results, including comparisons between Xen virtualization modes, container runtimes, and performance behavior of Kubernetes distributions. Finally, Section 6 gives the final remarks and outlines some future research directions.
